ai.title: Bronchogenic Carcinoma
ai.subject: Pathology
ai.summary: Bronchogenic carcinoma is a malignant tumour of the bronchial epithelium, most often linked to smoking and asbestos exposure. In low‑resource settings, co‑existing TB, HIV and chronic lung disease modify presentation and diagnostic options.

sections.p: A malignant tumour arising from the bronchial epithelium, confirmed by histology of a tissue sample. Diagnosis rests on imaging, cytology or biopsy, with the aim to identify tumour type (small‑cell vs non‑small‑cell) and stage.
b: Histology (sputum cytology, bronchoscopy biopsy, CT‑guided needle) confirms malignancy
Imaging (CXR, chest CT) shows mass, cavitation, lymphadenopathy

t.b: Does a mass or suspicious opacity exist? – Shows size, location, possible cavitation; if unavailable, proceed to clinical suspicion and refer for CT when possible
What is the tumour size, nodal involvement, and distant spread? – Provides TNM staging; if CT not available, use ultrasound for supraclavicular nodes and plain X‑ray patterns
Is the lesion histologically malignant and what is the cell type? – Gives definitive diagnosis; if bronchoscopy unavailable, consider percutaneous needle biopsy or sputum cytology

sections.p: Staging follows the TNM system (AJCC 8th edition). Stage determines resectability and guides therapy.
b: T – tumour size and invasion of adjacent structures
N – regional lymph node involvement
M – distant metastasis

t.b: What is the T and N status? – Defines local extent; if CT unavailable, use clinical assessment of chest wall fixation and supraclavicular node exam
Is there skeletal metastasis? – Detects M1 disease; if not available, look for bone pain and elevated alkaline phosphatase

sections.p: The dominant risk is tobacco smoking, amplified by asbestos, silica, and chronic lung inflammation common in low‑resource settings.
b: Cigarette smoking (≥20 pack‑years) – strongest risk factor
Asbestos exposure – synergistic with smoking
Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) – provides field for malignant transformation
Pulmonary tuberculosis (especially post‑TB scarring) – prevalent in East Africa
HIV infection – immunosuppression increases risk of aggressive subtypes

sections.p: Patients often present with a cough, haemoptysis, weight loss and chest pain. In resource‑limited settings, symptoms may be masked by endemic TB or chronic bronchitis.
b: Persistent cough >3 weeks
Haemoptysis (fresh blood or blood‑streaked sputum)
Unexplained weight loss and anorexia
Chest pain, often pleuritic
Dyspnoea on exertion

sections.p: Select tests that answer specific clinical questions while recognising limited availability.

t.b: Is malignant cells present in expectorated material? – Positive result supports diagnosis; negative does not rule out cancer
Are peripheral nodes enlarged and accessible for fine‑needle aspiration? – Provides tissue when bronchoscopy unavailable
Do values suggest small‑cell carcinoma or bone metastasis? – Elevated LDH may point to small‑cell; hypercalcaemia suggests squamous cell

sections.p: Complications arise from local invasion, metastasis and treatment‑related effects.
b: Massive haemoptysis – airway emergency
Superior vena cava syndrome – facial swelling, venous distension
Spinal cord compression – back pain, neurological deficit
Pleural effusion – dyspnoea, dullness to percussion

sections.p: Treatment is multidisciplinary; in low‑resource hospitals, focus on curative surgery when feasible, otherwise palliative chemo‑radiotherapy and symptom control.
b: Surgical resection (lobectomy, pneumonectomy) for stage I‑II non‑small‑cell carcinoma, if operative risk acceptable
Platinum‑based doublet chemotherapy (cisplatin + gemcitabine or paclitaxel) for stage III‑IV NSCLC; avoid if renal failure or severe neuropathy
Concurrent chemoradiation for locally advanced disease; radiotherapy may be limited to 30 Gy in palliative settings
Supportive care: analgesia, bronchodilators, oxygen, management of haemoptysis with topical epinephrine or bronchial artery embolisation if available

sections.p: Long‑term surveillance detects recurrence; primary prevention targets smoking and occupational exposures.
b: Chest CT at 6 months then annually for 2 years after curative treatment
Smoking cessation counseling and nicotine‑replacement where possible
Vaccination against influenza and pneumococcus to reduce secondary infections
Screen high‑risk individuals (≥30 pack‑years, age ≥55) with low‑dose CT if resources allow

sections.p: Several pulmonary conditions mimic bronchogenic carcinoma clinically and radiologically.
b: Pulmonary tuberculosis – cavitary lesions, weight loss, haemoptysis; differentiate by sputum GeneXpert and response to anti‑TB therapy
Bronchiectasis – chronic purulent sputum, tram‑track opacities; CT shows dilated airways
Lung abscess – thick‑walled cavity with air‑fluid level; responds to antibiotics

sections.p: Interpretation pitfalls are common when resources are limited.
b: Normal chest X‑ray does not exclude early tumour; rely on clinical suspicion
Negative sputum cytology may be false‑negative; repeat or obtain tissue
Elevated CA‑125 or CEA are non‑specific; do not use alone for diagnosis

whenToSeekHelp: Sudden onset of severe dyspnoea or chest pain
Signs of superior vena cava syndrome

faq.q: Why is smoking such a strong risk factor?
faq.a: Carcinogens in tobacco cause DNA damage in bronchial epithelium, leading to mutations that drive malignant transformation.

faq.q: Can a patient with treated TB still develop bronchogenic carcinoma?
faq.a: Yes; scar tissue from healed TB creates a field of chronic inflammation that predisposes to cancer.

faq.q: Is a single negative bronchoscopy enough to rule out cancer?
faq.a: No; sampling error is possible. Repeat biopsy or alternative tissue acquisition is required if suspicion remains.

exam: A 58‑year‑old smoker presents with a 2‑month cough and weight loss; CXR shows a peripheral mass. What is the next diagnostic step and why? — Answer: Obtain tissue (bronchoscopy or CT‑guided biopsy) to confirm histology before planning treatment.

How does the presence of HIV infection alter the prognosis of bronchogenic carcinoma? — Answer: HIV‑related immunosuppression leads to more aggressive histologic subtypes and poorer survival, emphasizing early staging and treatment.

A patient with known NSCLC develops facial swelling and neck vein distension. What complication should you suspect and what immediate management is required? — Answer: Superior vena cava syndrome; elevate head, give steroids, and arrange urgent radiotherapy or stenting.

Why is platinum‑based chemotherapy preferred for advanced NSCLC in low‑resource settings? — Answer: It offers the best evidence of survival benefit, is relatively inexpensive, and can be combined with locally available agents.

What feature on CT distinguishes a cavitary TB lesion from a squamous‑cell carcinoma cavity? — Answer: TB cavities often have thick, irregular walls with surrounding infiltrates; cancer cavities tend to have nodular inner walls and may show adjacent lymphadenopathy.

A patient with stage IIIA NSCLC cannot undergo surgery. What is the standard curative‑intent treatment? — Answer: Concurrent chemoradiotherapy (platinum doublet plus 60 Gy), because it offers the highest chance of local control.

Explain why routine CA‑125 measurement is not useful in diagnosing lung cancer. — Answer: CA‑125 lacks specificity; it can be elevated in many benign conditions and does not change management without histologic confirmation.

In a setting without CT, how would you assess mediastinal lymph node involvement? — Answer: Perform thorough physical exam for supraclavicular nodes, use ultrasound‑guided fine‑needle aspiration, and consider mediastinoscopy if feasible.
